## 6. Distribution registry (the catalog)

Distinct from the runtime registry (§7). This is where packages live.

### 6.1 Package format

A plugin is a gzipped tar with a content-addressed digest:

```
com.acme.snowflake-2.3.1.tgz
├── plugin.json
├── dist/server.js            # bundled, no node_modules resolution at runtime
├── dist/client.js            # ESM, bundled
├── schemas/*.json
├── assets/*
├── sbom.spdx.json
└── LICENSE
```

**Plugins ship bundled.** No `node_modules` tree, no install-time dependency resolution, no
postinstall scripts — ever. Bundling at publish time is what makes the artifact reproducible and the
SBOM meaningful, and it eliminates the entire class of "works on my machine" and
"transitive dep changed under us" failures. Native addons are the one exception and require
platform-team sign-off plus per-platform artifacts (`runtime.server.nativeTargets`).

### 6.2 API

```
GET  /v1/plugins                                  list, filter by extension point / channel
GET  /v1/plugins/{id}                             metadata, all versions
GET  /v1/plugins/{id}/versions/{ver}/manifest     manifest only (cheap, for resolution)
GET  /v1/plugins/{id}/versions/{ver}/package      the tarball (redirect to CDN/OCI)
POST /v1/plugins/{id}/versions                    publish (signed, CI identity only)
POST /v1/plugins/{id}/versions/{ver}/yank         yank (see below)
GET  /v1/index                                    full index, ETag'd, for air-gapped mirroring
```

### 6.3 Channels and promotion

`canary` → `beta` → `stable`. A version is promoted, not republished — the digest is identical
across channels, which is what lets you prove the thing you tested is the thing you shipped. Tenants
subscribe to a channel per plugin; default `stable`.

### 6.4 Yanking vs. deleting

**Versions are never deleted.** Yanking marks a version un-installable for *new* installs and raises
an operator alert on existing ones; it does not auto-uninstall, because silently removing a data
source breaks every report that used it. A yank carries a reason and a severity: `security` yanks
additionally open an incident and, for `critical`, allow the platform team to force-quarantine
(§8.7) across tenants. That force path is audited and requires two-person approval.

### 6.5 Air-gapped installs

Self-hosted customers mirror `/v1/index` plus tarballs. The signature chain is verified against a
pinned public key baked into the host image, so mirroring does not require trusting the mirror.

## 7. Runtime registry

The in-process index of what's installed and what it can do. This is the component the rest of the
host talks to.

### 7.1 Data model

```ts
interface PluginRecord {
  id: PluginId;
  version: SemVer;
  manifest: Manifest;                  // validated, migrated to current manifestVersion
  source: { channel: Channel; digest: string; installedAt: Date; installedBy: PrincipalId };
  state: LifecycleState;               // §8.1
  stateReason?: { code: ErrorCode; message: string; at: Date };
  grants: PermissionGrant[];           // what the operator actually approved (⊆ manifest asks)
  instances: InstanceRef[];            // one per tenant pool (§14)
  health: { crashes: CrashRecord[]; breaker: BreakerState; lastHealthyAt?: Date };
  contributions: ContributionRecord[];
}

interface ContributionRecord {
  fqid: string;                        // com.acme.snowflake/datasource/snowflake
  point: ExtensionPointId;
  pluginId: PluginId;
  order: number;                       // §7.2
  enabled: boolean;                    // tenant-level toggle
  spec: unknown;                       // point-specific, schema-validated
}
```

### 7.2 The contribution index

`Map<ExtensionPointId, ContributionRecord[]>`, kept sorted. Identity collisions are impossible
(§4.2), so ordering is the only policy needed, and it must be **deterministic across restarts and
across nodes in a cluster** — otherwise two app servers render the same report differently, which is
a genuinely miserable bug to chase.

Sort key, in order: `(explicit operator order ASC, manifest priority ASC, pluginId ASC, localId ASC)`.
The tail of that key is total and stable, so ties never fall through to insertion order.

### 7.3 Resolution

```
resolve(query) → ContributionRecord
  1. Look up by fqid; if absent, fail E_EXTENSION_NOT_FOUND (report names the missing plugin ID —
     this becomes a user-facing "install the Snowflake plugin" prompt, not a stack trace).
  2. Check the saved report's authored-against major vs the installed major.
     Same major        → proceed.
     Installed newer   → proceed, emit a compat-warning annotation on the report.
     Installed older   → fail E_API_INCOMPATIBLE with both versions named.
  3. Check tenant enablement (§14) and operator grants.
  4. Return.
```

Plugin-to-plugin dependencies are resolved at **install** time, not at load: the installer walks
`dependencies.plugins`, checks each is installed and satisfies the range, rejects on cycle or on
depth > 2. There is no backtracking and no automatic co-installation — if a dep is missing, the
install fails with an actionable message. This is a deliberate 10% of npm's power for 1% of its
complexity, and for five internal teams it is the right trade.

### 7.4 Reconciliation

The registry does not mutate plugin processes directly. Desired state lives in the database
(`installed_plugins`, `plugin_grants`, `tenant_plugin_enablement`); a reconciler loop diffs desired
against actual and drives the supervisor. This is the standard controller pattern and it buys us
three things: crash recovery is just "reconcile on boot", cluster nodes converge independently
without a coordination protocol, and every state transition has one code path to test.

```
every 5s, and on change notification:
  desired = db.desiredState(nodeId)
  actual  = supervisor.actualState()
  for each diff:
    install / uninstall / activate / deactivate / upgrade / quarantine
  emit reconcile_lag metric
```

## 8. Lifecycle

### 8.1 State machine

```
                    ┌──────────────┐
                    │  Discovered  │  manifest fetched, not yet validated
                    └──────┬───────┘
                           │ validate + verify signature
                    ┌──────▼───────┐
             ┌──────│   Resolved   │  deps satisfied, API compatible
             │      └──────┬───────┘
             │             │ operator approves grants
             │      ┌──────▼───────┐
             │      │  Installed   │  on disk, indexed, NOT running
             │      └──────┬───────┘
             │             │ activation event fires (or eager)
             │      ┌──────▼───────┐
             │      │  Activating  │  process spawned, handshake, activate() running
             │      └──────┬───────┘
             │             │ activate() resolved
             │      ┌──────▼───────┐
             │   ┌──│    Active    │◄─┐  serving calls
             │   │  └──────┬───────┘  │
             │   │         │ deactivate / reload / idle timeout
             │   │  ┌──────▼───────┐  │
             │   │  │ Deactivating │  │  draining in-flight (§8.4)
             │   │  └──────┬───────┘  │
             │   │         │          │ reload: re-activate
             │   │         └──────────┘
             │   │ crash
             │   │  ┌──────────────┐
             │   └─►│   Crashed    │──► backoff ──► Activating
             │      └──────┬───────┘
             │             │ breaker trips (N crashes in window)
             │      ┌──────▼───────┐
             └─────►│ Quarantined  │  contributions hidden, no restarts, operator alert
                    └──────────────┘
                    ┌──────────────┐
                    │    Failed    │  terminal for this version; validation/compat failure
                    └──────────────┘
```

Every transition is logged with `(pluginId, version, from, to, reason, traceId)` and emitted as a
metric. `Quarantined` and `Failed` page nobody by default but surface in the admin UI and in the
report-run error if a report depended on that plugin.

### 8.2 Hooks

The plugin implements at most these. All are optional except `activate`.

```ts
export interface PluginModule {
  activate(ctx: PluginContext): void | Promise<void>;
  deactivate?(reason: DeactivateReason): void | Promise<void>;
  onConfigChange?(next: Config, prev: Config): void | Promise<void>;
  onUpgrade?(from: SemVer, to: SemVer, store: MigrationStore): Promise<void>;
  healthCheck?(): Promise<HealthStatus>;
}
```

`DeactivateReason` is `'shutdown' | 'reload' | 'uninstall' | 'idle' | 'quarantine' | 'upgrade'`, and
plugins are expected to branch on it — flushing a write buffer is right for `shutdown`, pointless
for `quarantine`.

**Install/uninstall hooks do not exist, by design.** A plugin that runs code at install time is a
plugin that can fail at install time in ways an operator can't debug, and it's the mechanism behind
most real-world package-manager compromises. Anything you'd want in `onInstall` belongs in
`activate` guarded by a first-run check in `ctx.storage`.

### 8.3 Load (activation)

Activation is lazy by default. `activation.events` declares what wakes a plugin:

| Event | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `onDataSource:<fqid>` | A report run needs that data source |
| `onExtension:<fqid>` | Generic: any contribution is resolved |
| `onSchedule` | A trigger window opens |
| `onStartup` | Eager. Requires sign-off; counts against a per-tenant eager budget. |

```
activate(pluginId):
  1. supervisor.ensureProcess(pluginId)        spawn if cold; §9.1.2 for what the process gets
  2. handshake                                 API version negotiation + capability list (§11.2)
  3. broker.mintCapabilities(grants)           only what was granted; handles, not ambient access
  4. rpc.call('activate', ctx)                 deadline: activation.timeoutMs (default 10s)
  5. collect registrations                     everything registered during activate() is bound
                                               to the plugin's DisposableStore
  6. state → Active; index contributions; emit plugin_activation_duration_ms
```

Activation is **idempotent and single-flight**: concurrent report runs that both need a cold plugin
join the same activation promise. Getting this wrong produces double-spawn under load, which is the
classic way plugin systems blow their memory budget during a traffic spike.

### 8.4 Unload (deactivation)

Unload is where most plugin architectures quietly fail, so it gets the most machinery:

```
deactivate(pluginId, reason):
  1. registry: mark contributions unavailable   → no NEW calls routed here
  2. drain: wait for in-flight calls            → deadline = min(remaining call deadlines, 30s)
  3. rpc.call('deactivate', reason)             → deadline 5s
  4. broker.revokeAll(pluginId)                 → capability handles die; any in-flight host call
                                                  using them fails E_PERMISSION_REVOKED
  5. disposables.disposeAll()                   → host-side registrations released
  6. supervisor.stopProcess(pluginId)           → SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 5s
  7. state → Installed
```

Steps 4–6 are the reason for process isolation. **In-process unload cannot be made correct**: a
plugin that called `setInterval` and lost the handle, opened a socket in a native addon, or captured
a reference in a module-level closure will leak past any `delete require.cache` you attempt. Step 6
makes unload a guarantee rather than a hope — the OS reclaims everything. Anything we build that
isn't backed by `kill(pid)` is best-effort by construction.

Host-side leak defense, for the parts we *can* control: every host API that creates a registration
returns a `Disposable`, and `ctx.subscriptions` auto-disposes on deactivate. `ctx.signal` (an
`AbortSignal`) fires at step 3 so well-behaved plugins can cancel their own work cooperatively.

### 8.5 Reload

Reload = deactivate + activate, with two refinements:

- **State handoff.** `deactivate('reload')` may return a JSON-serializable blob (≤ 256 KB) that is
  passed to the next `activate` as `ctx.previousState`. Intended for warm caches and connection
  pool hints — never for correctness-critical state, because reload can fail between the two halves
  and the blob is dropped. The contract says so explicitly and the conformance kit tests a plugin's
  behavior when `previousState` is absent.
- **Drain-before-swap for upgrades.** For version upgrades the supervisor can run old and new
  processes concurrently: new process activates, registry atomically swaps routing, old process
  drains and exits. Report runs in flight finish on the old version. This is opt-in per plugin via
  `lifecycle.concurrentUpgrade: true` (default false), because it requires the plugin to tolerate two
  instances against the same external system — which, for something holding an exclusive lock or a
  single-writer connection, it may not.

**Dev-mode hot reload.** A file watcher on an unpacked plugin directory triggers reload on change,
typically 200–400 ms end to end. This is the single highest-leverage DX feature in the system and it
falls out of the design for free because unload actually works.

### 8.6 Crash supervision

```
on process exit (unexpected):
  record crash (exit code, signal, last 64 KB of stderr, in-flight call IDs)
  fail in-flight calls with E_PLUGIN_CRASHED (retryable: true if the call was idempotent)
  if breaker.shouldTrip():  state → Quarantined; alert
  else:                     backoff = min(1s * 2^n, 60s) ± 20% jitter; state → Activating
```

Breaker: 5 crashes in 10 minutes, or 3 consecutive crashes within 30 s of activation (crash-loop).
The second condition matters — a plugin that dies immediately on activation would otherwise burn the
full backoff schedule before tripping.

Idempotency: `query`, `describe`, `plan`, and `testConnection` are declared idempotent and are
retried once on crash. `apply` (transforms) is retried only if the plugin declares
`transform.pure: true`. `destination.deliver` is **never** auto-retried without an
`idempotencyKey` — double-emailing a board report is worse than failing.

### 8.7 Quarantine

A quarantined plugin: contributions hidden from resolution, no restarts attempted, existing reports
that reference it fail with a message naming the plugin and the reason, and an operator alert fires.
Exit requires an explicit operator action or an upgrade to a different version. Quarantine state is
per-node-pool but recorded centrally, so a plugin crash-looping on one node doesn't silently keep
serving from another.

## 9. The sandbox

### 9.1 Server surface

#### 9.1.1 Decision: separate OS process. Not `vm`, not `vm2`, not worker threads.

This is the load-bearing decision in the whole design, so here is the reasoning in full:

- **Node's `vm` module is explicitly not a security boundary.** Node's own documentation says so.
  Escapes via constructor-chain walking (`this.constructor.constructor('return process')()`) are
  trivial and have been rediscovered continuously for a decade.
- **`vm2` is dead.** It was the widely-used hardened alternative; it was discontinued in 2023 after
  a series of sandbox-escape CVEs its author judged unfixable in the design. Anything built on it
  today is building on a known-broken foundation.
- **Worker threads share the process.** Better than `vm` — you get `resourceLimits` for heap — but a
  worker can still call `process.exit()`, and a native addon segfault takes down the whole process
  including the host. For a system whose first requirement is "a broken plugin cannot break the
  host", that's disqualifying.
- **A separate process gives us what we actually need**: OS-enforced memory limits, real CPU
  accounting, kill-means-kill unload, crash containment including native code, and a natural place
  to drop privileges.

The cost is IPC serialization on the hot path, which is exactly why §10.4 exists.

#### 9.1.2 What a plugin process gets

One process per plugin (not per tenant — see §14 for the tenant story), spawned by the supervisor:

- **Clean environment.** Empty `env` except an explicit allowlist (`NODE_ENV`, `TZ`, `LANG`, and a
  process-specific `PLUGIN_CHANNEL_FD`). No inherited secrets, no `AWS_*`, no proxy vars.
- **Reduced privileges.** Linux: dedicated uid, `no_new_privs`, seccomp profile blocking
  `socket(2)`/`connect(2)` outright (all network goes through the broker — §9.5), cgroup v2 for
  memory and CPU, read-only rootfs with a per-plugin tmpfs. Windows: Job Object with
  `ProcessMemoryLimit`, `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE`, `ActiveProcessLimit = 1`, restricted
  token, and a per-plugin temp directory. macOS (dev only): `sandbox-exec` profile.
- **Node flags.** `--max-old-space-size` matched to `resources.memoryMb`, `--disallow-code-generation-from-strings`,
  `--frozen-intrinsics`, `--no-experimental-fetch` (fetch comes from the broker), and a
  `--experimental-permission` policy denying fs/net/child_process as defense in depth.
- **No stdio to the console.** stdout/stderr are captured, line-bounded, rate-limited, and forwarded
  as structured log records tagged with the plugin ID. A plugin that logs 100 MB/s gets throttled and
  flagged, not allowed to fill the node's disk.

The plugin process *enforces nothing*. It is untrusted. Every limit above is imposed from outside by
the OS or the host. That's the property that makes the boundary real.

#### 9.1.3 Resource governance

| Limit | Mechanism | On breach |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | cgroup / Job Object, plus `--max-old-space-size` | OOM-kill → crash path (§8.6) |
| CPU | cgroup `cpu.max` / Job Object CPU rate | Throttle; sustained → `E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` |
| Wall clock per call | Host-side deadline timer | Cancel, `E_TIMEOUT`, strike |
| Concurrency | Host-side semaphore per plugin | Queue, then `E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` |
| Egress bytes | Broker accounting (§9.5) | Hard stop mid-stream |
| Result rows | Data plane counter (§10.4) | Hard stop, `E_RESULT_TOO_LARGE` |
| Log volume | Token bucket on the log forwarder | Drop + flag |
| Process count | `ActiveProcessLimit` / cgroup pids | `fork` fails inside the plugin |

**Three timeout strikes within a 5-minute window recycles the process.** A plugin that times out
repeatedly is usually leaking or deadlocked, and recycling is cheaper than diagnosing it live.

#### 9.1.4 WASM tier (designed, Phase 4)

For a future `community` tier: compile plugins to WASM components and run them in a host-side
runtime with WASI Preview 2. Capability-based by construction, deterministic, memory-safe,
millisecond cold start, and no OS-level trust required. The reason it isn't v1: the toolchain for
"write TypeScript, get a WASM component" (via Componentize-JS / StarlingMonkey) is workable but the
ecosystem story for a data connector that wants a mature database driver is not. The API contract in
§11 is deliberately WASM-shaped — no shared mutable state, everything through explicit capability
handles, all data as serializable buffers — so this port is additive rather than a rewrite. **Do not
add a host API that takes a callback with shared state; it closes this door.**

### 9.2 Client surface

Visualizations run in the browser, and the threat model there is different: the risk is not resource
exhaustion but access to the host page — session cookies, other tenants' rendered data, the DOM of
the surrounding app.

**Mechanism: sandboxed iframe on a unique null origin.**

```html
<iframe
  sandbox="allow-scripts"                          <!-- NOT allow-same-origin: null origin -->
  csp="default-src 'none'; script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; img-src data: blob:"
  referrerpolicy="no-referrer"
  allow=""                                          <!-- no camera, geolocation, clipboard, … -->
  src="https://plugin-cdn.example/com.acme.snowflake/2.3.1/frame.html">
</iframe>
```

Critically, `allow-scripts` **without** `allow-same-origin`. Including both is the classic mistake:
together they let the frame reach out and remove its own sandbox attribute from the parent. With a
null origin the frame has no cookies, no `localStorage` shared with the app, and no DOM access
across the boundary.

- **Separate CDN origin per plugin**, so that even if `allow-same-origin` is ever needed for a
  specific plugin (canvas/WebGL edge cases), the origin isolation still holds.
- **Communication is `postMessage` only**, same envelope as §10, with strict origin checks on both
  ends and a per-frame nonce established at handshake.
- **Data reaches the frame as Arrow IPC `ArrayBuffer`s**, transferred (zero-copy) not cloned.
- **Rendering budget.** The host measures frame time; a visualization that exceeds
  `resources.frameBudgetMs` for N consecutive frames is suspended with a user-visible "this
  visualization is slow" state rather than freezing the report.
- **No network from the client surface, ever.** CSP `default-src 'none'` and no `connect-src`. If a
  visualization needs data, it asks the host over `postMessage` and the host fetches it. This is
  non-negotiable: a chart that can make arbitrary requests carrying the user's session is a
  data-exfiltration primitive.

Interactivity (tooltips, brush-select, drill-down) goes host-ward over the same channel, so the host
stays in control of navigation and of what a click can trigger.

### 9.3 Capability broker

Plugins get **no ambient authority**. Every external interaction is via a capability handle minted by
the host at activation, scoped to the grants the operator approved, and revoked at deactivation.

```ts
// A plugin never constructs these. They arrive on ctx, already scoped.
interface HttpCapability {
  fetch(req: PluginRequest): Promise<PluginResponse>;   // host-side allowlist + accounting
}
interface StorageCapability {
  get(key: string): Promise<Uint8Array | undefined>;    // namespaced to (plugin, tenant), quota'd
  set(key: string, value: Uint8Array, opts?: { ttlSec?: number }): Promise<void>;
  list(prefix: string): AsyncIterable<string>;
}
```

Handles are revocable by construction: the host holds the real implementation, the plugin holds a
proxy ID. Revocation flips a bit host-side, so a plugin that stashed a handle in a closure gains
nothing after deactivation. This also means revocation works even against a plugin process that
ignores its `AbortSignal`.

### 9.4 Secrets

Three access modes, declared per secret in the manifest. **`broker` is the default and the strong
recommendation**, and the conformance kit warns on `plaintext`.

| Mode | What the plugin gets | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `broker` | Nothing. Plugin says "sign this request with `snowflake.credentials`"; the host injects the credential at the egress proxy. | Almost always |
| `token` | A short-lived (≤ 15 min), narrowly scoped token minted by the host | Plugin must talk to an SDK that needs a credential object |
| `plaintext` | The secret value | Last resort. Requires platform-team sign-off recorded in the manifest. |

Under `broker`, a plugin that is fully compromised still cannot exfiltrate the credential — it can
only cause requests to the allowlisted host, which is a dramatically smaller problem. Secrets are
never in env vars, never in the manifest, never on the plugin's stdio, and are redacted from plugin
logs and error messages by a host-side scrubber keyed on the actual secret values.

### 9.5 Egress proxy

All plugin network traffic goes through a host-side proxy. Since the plugin process can't call
`connect(2)` at all (§9.1.2), this is enforced by the OS, not by the plugin's cooperation.

The proxy: matches the request against the manifest's egress allowlist (exact host or single-level
wildcard — no bare `*`), blocks private/link-local address ranges after DNS resolution to stop
SSRF-by-DNS-rebinding, pins TLS where a plugin declares a pin, injects brokered credentials, counts
bytes against the per-run cap, enforces per-plugin rate limits, and writes an audit record per
request `(plugin, tenant, host, bytes, status, traceId)`.

## 10. Wire protocol

### 10.1 Transport

| Surface | Transport |
|---|---|
| Server, Linux/macOS | Unix domain socket pair, inherited FD |
| Server, Windows | Named pipe (`\\.\pipe\reporting-plugin-<uuid>`) |
| Client | `postMessage` with `Transferable`s |

Framing: 4-byte big-endian length prefix + payload. Max control frame 8 MB (bulk data goes on the
data plane, §10.4).

### 10.2 Control plane

JSON-RPC 2.0 shape, MessagePack encoding (≈2–4× faster and smaller than JSON for our payloads, and
it has a real binary type, which matters when every result carries Arrow buffers).

```jsonc
// host → plugin
{ "id": 42, "method": "datasource.query",
  "params": { "connectionRef": "cap:conn:7f3a", "query": { … } },
  "meta": { "traceId": "…", "spanId": "…", "tenantId": "t_123",
            "deadlineUnixMs": 1737000030000, "apiVersion": "1.4" } }

// plugin → host (capability call, same channel, reversed direction)
{ "id": 1001, "method": "host.http.fetch",
  "params": { "capability": "cap:http:a91c", "request": { … } } }

// error
{ "id": 42, "error": { "code": "E_UPSTREAM", "message": "Snowflake: warehouse suspended",
                       "retryable": true, "retryAfterMs": 5000,
                       "userMessage": "The warehouse is paused. Ask your admin to resume it.",
                       "details": { … } } }
```

Bidirectional on one channel, with independent ID spaces per direction. Deadlines are **absolute
timestamps, not durations**, so a queued call doesn't get a fresh budget — a subtle but important
detail for avoiding deadline amplification in chained calls.

### 10.3 Cancellation

`$cancel` notification carries the target call ID. The plugin is expected to abort and reply with
`E_CANCELLED`; the host does not wait forever for that courtesy — at deadline + 2 s grace it
abandons the call, and at three abandonments the process is recycled (§9.1.3). Cancellation
propagates transitively: cancelling a report run cancels every in-flight plugin call under that
`traceId`.

### 10.4 Data plane

**This is the part that makes or breaks a reporting tool's plugin system**, and it's why the design
doesn't just use JSON-RPC for everything.

- **Format: Apache Arrow IPC stream.** Columnar, zero-copy-readable, language-agnostic, with a real
  type system including decimals and timestamps-with-timezone. A reporting tool's plugin boundary
  moves tabular data; using JSON for it costs roughly an order of magnitude in both CPU and bytes.
- **Batched.** Default 64K rows or 16 MB per `RecordBatch`, whichever comes first.
- **Credit-based backpressure.** The consumer grants credits (batches it's ready for); the producer
  may not send beyond its credit. Without this, a fast data source streaming into a slow transform
  buffers unboundedly in the host, and you learn about it via an OOM at 2 a.m.
- **Schema is sent once**, at stream open; batches carry only data.
- **Big payloads use shared memory** where available (`memfd` on Linux, named shared memory on
  Windows) with the control frame carrying only a handle — so a 16 MB batch crosses the boundary as
  a pointer, not a copy. This is what claws back most of the cost of process isolation.

```
host                                        plugin
 │── query(req) ───────────────────────────►│
 │◄── $stream.open { streamId, schema } ────│
 │── $stream.credit { streamId, n: 4 } ─────►│
 │◄── $stream.batch { streamId, shm: … } ───│  ×4
 │── $stream.credit { streamId, n: 4 } ─────►│
 │        …                                  │
 │◄── $stream.end { streamId, rows, stats } ─│
```

Streams are cancellable, deadline-bounded, and counted against the plugin's row and byte caps.

## 11. Versioned API contract

### 11.1 What is versioned

**The host API version** (`@reporting/plugin-api`) is one semver number covering: the `PluginContext`
surface, every extension point interface, the wire protocol, and the error taxonomy. One number, not
per-extension-point versioning — five teams should have to reason about one compatibility question,
not nine.

| Change | Bump |
|---|---|
| New extension point; new optional method; new optional field; new error code | **minor** |
| Remove/rename anything; change a parameter type; tighten validation; change semantics of an existing call | **major** |
| Docs, perf, bug fix that doesn't change the contract | patch |

**Support window: current major N and N−1, for a minimum of two quarters after N ships.** That's the
promise to the five teams — you get at least six months to migrate, and never a forced same-sprint
upgrade.

### 11.2 Negotiation handshake

```
host → plugin:  { hostApiVersions: ["1.4", "2.1"],       // majors supported, at their current minor
                  capabilities: ["datasource.streaming", "secrets.broker", "data.shm", …],
                  hostVersion: "2026.9.1" }

plugin → host:  { selected: "1.4",
                  requires: ["datasource.streaming", "secrets.broker"],
                  provides: ["datasource", "panel-editor"],
                  sdkVersion: "1.4.2" }

host:           verify selected ∈ offered ∧ manifest.api.host satisfies selected
                verify requires ⊆ capabilities
                else → E_API_INCOMPATIBLE, state → Failed, actionable message naming both versions
```

The handshake is the **only** place version negotiation happens. No per-call version fields, no
runtime sniffing of host internals. A plugin that can't get what it needs fails loudly at activation
rather than subtly at report-render time.

### 11.3 Capability flags: how additive change actually works

Within a major, new functionality arrives as a **capability flag**, never as a silent behavior
change. A plugin feature-detects:

```ts
if (ctx.hasCapability('datasource.costEstimate')) {
  registry.registerDataSource({ …spec, estimateCost });
}
```

This is what lets one plugin build run against host 1.4 and host 1.9 without conditionals on version
strings — which are always wrong eventually, because the thing you care about is the feature, not
the number.

### 11.4 Deprecation

```
minor N     → mark @deprecated in the .d.ts with a replacement and a removal version.
              Runtime: one-time structured warning per plugin per process. Never a throw.
minor N+1   → warning also surfaces in the admin UI and in the plugin's health status.
major N+1   → removed. Migration guide + codemod published at the time of the deprecation,
              not at removal.
```

**Minimum two minors and one full quarter between deprecation and removal.** No exceptions without
an RFC and direct notice to every affected plugin owner — the catalog knows who they are, so "we
didn't know who was using it" is never an acceptable answer.

### 11.5 Mechanical enforcement

Care doesn't scale to five teams. CI enforces:

1. **API extractor** rolls the public surface into a single `.api.md` report, committed to the repo.
2. A PR that changes that file **fails** unless it also bumps the version appropriately and carries a
   `api-change:minor|major` label with an RFC link for major.
3. **Semver linting** (`api-extractor` + a custom rule) classifies the diff and cross-checks the
   declared bump against the actual change. A removed method on a `minor` bump is a hard failure.
4. **Compatibility matrix in CI**: every plugin in the catalog's `stable` channel is run against the
   host's `main` conformance suite nightly. Breaking the five teams shows up as a red build on *our*
   repo, not as their incident.
5. **Protocol golden files**: recorded wire traces replay against new host builds to catch
   serialization-level breakage the type system can't see.

Item 4 is the one that actually keeps the promise. Everything else catches mistakes; that catches
consequences.

## 12. Errors and observability

### 12.1 Taxonomy

| Code | Retryable | Who's at fault | Surfaced as |
|---|---|---|---|
| `E_MANIFEST_INVALID` | no | plugin author | Publish/install failure |
| `E_API_INCOMPATIBLE` | no | author or operator | Install/activation failure, both versions named |
| `E_PERMISSION_DENIED` | no | operator (missing grant) | Admin prompt to grant |
| `E_PERMISSION_REVOKED` | no | lifecycle race | Internal; retry after reactivation |
| `E_USER_CONFIG` | no | end user | Inline field error in the editor |
| `E_UPSTREAM` | usually | external system | "Snowflake is unavailable", with retry-after |
| `E_TIMEOUT` | yes | plugin or upstream | "Timed out after 30s", names the plugin |
| `E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` | maybe | plugin or query | "Result too large — add a filter" |
| `E_RESULT_TOO_LARGE` | no | end user | Actionable: row cap and current count |
| `E_PLUGIN_CRASHED` | if idempotent | plugin author | Generic user message + operator alert |
| `E_CANCELLED` | n/a | — | Silent |
| `E_INTERNAL` | no | platform | Generic user message + our alert |

**Two messages per error, always.** `userMessage` is end-user-safe, actionable, and free of internal
detail; `message` + `details` go to operators and logs. A plugin that puts a connection string in
`userMessage` fails conformance. Host-side redaction scrubs known secret values from both as a
backstop, since conformance tests can't catch every path.

### 12.2 Telemetry

Everything is tagged `(pluginId, pluginVersion, extensionPoint, tenantId, traceId)`.

**Metrics.** `plugin_call_duration_ms` (histogram, by method), `plugin_call_errors_total` (by code),
`plugin_activation_duration_ms`, `plugin_memory_rss_bytes`, `plugin_cpu_seconds_total`,
`plugin_crashes_total`, `plugin_egress_bytes_total`, `plugin_rows_emitted_total`,
`plugin_stream_credit_wait_ms` (backpressure visibility — the early warning for a slow plugin),
`plugin_state` (gauge by state).

**Tracing.** The host's span context propagates into the plugin via `meta`, and `ctx.telemetry`
lets a plugin open child spans. A report run's trace therefore shows host planning, plugin query,
upstream latency, and transform time as one tree — which is the difference between "the report is
slow" and "the Snowflake plugin spends 8 seconds in DNS."

**Per-plugin dashboards are generated**, not hand-built: every plugin gets the same dashboard from a
template at install. Five teams, five identical debugging experiences.

## 13. Configuration

Two levels, both schema-driven:

- **Plugin settings** — operator-scoped, validated against `manifest.configuration` (JSON Schema).
  The admin UI is generated from that schema, so plugins don't ship settings UIs for simple cases.
  Changes deliver via `onConfigChange`; a plugin that doesn't implement it gets reloaded instead.
- **Connection/instance config** — end-user-scoped, validated against the contribution's
  `connectionSchema`. Fields marked `"x-secret": true` are routed to the secret store and replaced
  with a reference before they ever reach the plugin.

Config is versioned alongside the plugin: `onUpgrade` receives a `MigrationStore` for rewriting
stored config between versions, run once per tenant, transactionally, with the old config retained
for one version so a rollback is possible.

## 14. Multi-tenancy

The question that determines the cost model: **one plugin process per tenant, or shared?**

**Decision: shared process, tenant-scoped calls, with a pinning escape hatch.**

- Default: one process per `(plugin, node)`, serving all tenants. Every call carries `tenantId` in
  `meta`; every capability handle is tenant-scoped, so `ctx.storage` for tenant A physically cannot
  read tenant B's keys — the namespacing is host-side, not a convention the plugin must follow.
- Per-tenant processes are one order of magnitude more expensive at our tenant count and buy a
  boundary we already get from capability scoping for everything except *in-memory* cross-tenant
  leakage within a single plugin process.
- That residual risk is real: a plugin with a module-level cache keyed carelessly could serve
  tenant A's data to tenant B. Mitigations: the conformance kit includes a cross-tenant isolation
  test (interleaved calls with distinct tenants, asserting no data crossover), and the API makes the
  right thing easy — `ctx.storage` and `ctx.cache` are tenant-scoped by default, so a plugin has to
  go out of its way to build a global cache.
- **Pinning escape hatch:** `isolation: "per-tenant"` in the manifest, or per-tenant policy for
  regulated customers, gives a dedicated process. Costed and opt-in.

Tenant-level enablement lives in `tenant_plugin_enablement`; a plugin installed at the node level is
not automatically visible to every tenant.

## 15. Developer experience

This section is what makes five teams productive, and it should be resourced accordingly — a great
boundary with a bad dev loop produces five unhappy teams shipping late.

### 15.1 SDK

`@reporting/plugin-sdk` wraps `@reporting/plugin-api` with ergonomics: typed builders, an Arrow
helper layer (`rowsToBatches`, `batchesToRows` for small results), retry/backoff helpers, a
`DisposableStore`, and structured logging. The API package is the contract; the SDK is convenience
and may move faster. Plugins depend on both, and the SDK's major tracks the API's.

### 15.2 CLI

```
reporting-plugin init --template datasource      scaffold, with tests and CI wired up
reporting-plugin dev                             run in a local host with hot reload (§8.5)
reporting-plugin validate                        manifest + schema + lint, exactly as the catalog will
reporting-plugin test                            unit + conformance (§15.3)
reporting-plugin build                           bundle, generate SBOM
reporting-plugin publish --channel canary        sign (CI identity) and publish
reporting-plugin doctor                          diagnose permission/capability/version mismatches
```

`validate` running the *identical* code path as the catalog's publish check is the point — nobody
should discover a manifest problem at publish time.

### 15.3 Conformance kit

`@reporting/plugin-conformance` — a test suite a plugin runs in its own CI. This is the mechanism
that lets five teams ship without platform review of every change.

Suites: **lifecycle** (activate/deactivate idempotency, clean unload with no leaked handles, reload
with and without `previousState`, `deactivate` under every reason), **contract** (every declared
extension point implements its interface; declared pushdown capabilities are verified against a
reference implementation — §4.1), **isolation** (no ambient fs/net access; cross-tenant leakage
probe), **resilience** (behavior under injected upstream failure, timeout, cancellation mid-stream,
and host restart), **data** (Arrow schema correctness, null/decimal/timestamp-tz round-trip,
backpressure compliance, row-cap behavior), **hygiene** (no secrets in logs or `userMessage`; error
codes from the taxonomy; deprecation warnings clean).

Conformance is a **publish gate**: `stable` channel requires a green run against the target host
major. `canary` does not, so experimentation stays cheap.

### 15.4 Local dev loop

`reporting-plugin dev` starts a real host with a seeded sample dataset, the plugin loaded unpacked
with hot reload, an RPC inspector showing every frame crossing the boundary, and fault injection
(`--inject latency=500ms,error-rate=0.1`). Target: edit-to-visible under one second.

### 15.5 Docs

Generated API reference from TSDoc, plus hand-written guides per extension point, a migration guide
per major, and — most importantly — **three complete reference plugins** maintained by the platform
team as living examples: a data source (with pushdown), a transform (streaming, stateful), and a
visualization (client surface, interactive). These are the thing teams will actually copy, so they
must be exemplary and must stay current.

## 16. Governance

**Extension point ownership.** Each extension point has a named platform-team owner who reviews
changes to it. Ownership is in `CODEOWNERS` and enforced on the API package.

**RFC process.** Required for: a new extension point, any major bump, a new host capability, and any
change to the permission model. Template: motivation, API sketch, compatibility impact, migration
plan, alternatives. Two-week comment window with the five plugin teams explicitly on the reviewer
list. Not required for additive optional methods behind a capability flag — those are the intended
fast path, and making them cheap is what keeps the RFC process from being routed around.

**Plugin review gate.** `verified` tier requires: platform-team review of the manifest (permissions
and egress especially — the `reason` fields exist for this conversation), green conformance, signed
publish from CI identity only, and a named owner with an on-call rotation.

**Breaking-change council.** Before any major, the platform team and all five plugin owners meet,
review the compatibility matrix, and agree the timeline. The support window (§11.1) is a floor, not
a target.

**Deprecation registry.** A machine-readable list of every deprecated symbol with its removal
version, published in the catalog so a plugin's CI can fail on "you are using something that will be
gone in two quarters."

## 17. Rollout for the quarter

Five teams starting next quarter means the API surface they build against must be frozen before they
start, and the tooling must exist before their first PR. Sequenced accordingly:

| Phase | Window | Deliverable | Gate to exit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0 — Contract freeze** | Weeks −3 to 0 | `plugin-api@1.0.0`, manifest schema, this doc reviewed by all five teams | All five sign off on their extension points. **API frozen for the quarter at this point.** |
| **1 — Host core** | Weeks 1–4 | Registry, lifecycle, supervisor, process sandbox, control-plane RPC, `core`-tier in-process path | A reference data source loads, serves, unloads clean, survives induced crash |
| **2 — Data plane + client** | Weeks 3–7 | Arrow streaming with backpressure, shared memory, iframe sandbox, visualization point | 10M-row report streams end to end under the memory budget |
| **3 — DX + hardening** | Weeks 5–9 | CLI, conformance kit, dev loop, three reference plugins, catalog with signing | A team ships a plugin to `canary` with zero platform-team involvement |
| **4 — Production** | Weeks 8–12 | Egress proxy, secret broker, quarantine, telemetry, admin UI, multi-tenancy | Security review passed; first `stable` publish |
| **Post-Q** | — | WASM tier (§9.1.4), `community` trust tier, marketplace | — |

**Phases 1–3 deliberately overlap DX with host work.** Shipping the host first and the tooling later
is the standard way this goes wrong: five teams spend a month building against an API with no local
dev loop, and the feedback that would have improved the API arrives after it's frozen.

**Critical path, watch these:** contract freeze slipping (blocks all five teams), and the conformance
kit slipping (turns into manual platform-team review of every plugin, which does not scale past
about two teams).

## 18. Decisions and rejected alternatives

| # | Decision | Rejected | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | Separate OS process per plugin | `vm`/`vm2`; worker threads | `vm` is not a security boundary per Node's own docs; vm2 discontinued 2023 after unfixable escapes; workers can `process.exit()` and die to native segfaults. Only a process makes unload a guarantee. (§9.1.1) |
| D2 | Arrow IPC data plane, separate from control plane | JSON-RPC for everything | ~10× CPU and bytes on the path that matters most for a reporting tool. (§10.4) |
| D3 | Credit-based backpressure | Unbounded buffering; simple pause/resume | Unbounded buffering OOMs the host on fast-source/slow-sink; pause/resume is coarse and oscillates. |
| D4 | Bundled packages, no runtime dep resolution | npm install at plugin install | Reproducibility, meaningful SBOM, no postinstall attack surface. (§6.1) |
| D5 | Lazy activation by default | Eager | Startup time scales with plugin count; five teams ⇒ many plugins. Eager needs sign-off. |
| D6 | Capability handles, zero ambient authority | Permission checks at call sites | Check-at-call-site is a bug away from being forgotten; a plugin that has no handle cannot forget. Also keeps the WASM door open. (§9.3) |
| D7 | Shared process, tenant-scoped calls | Process per tenant | 10× cost for a boundary capability scoping already provides, except in-memory leakage — covered by conformance test + pinning escape hatch. (§14) |
| D8 | One API version for the whole surface | Per-extension-point versioning | Five teams should reason about one compatibility question. Capability flags give the granularity without the matrix. (§11.1) |
| D9 | Namespaced contribution IDs | Global IDs + conflict resolution | Makes collisions structurally impossible; only ordering needs policy. (§4.2) |
| D10 | No install/uninstall hooks | Full lifecycle hooks | Install-time code execution is the primary package-manager compromise vector and is undebuggable for operators. (§8.2) |
| D11 | Reconciler loop over direct mutation | Imperative install/activate calls | Free crash recovery, independent cluster convergence, one code path to test. (§7.4) |
| D12 | Secrets brokered, never handed over | Inject as env/config | A fully compromised plugin still can't exfiltrate the credential. (§9.4) |
| D13 | `allow-scripts` without `allow-same-origin` | Same-origin iframe; Shadow DOM | Both together let the frame unsandbox itself; Shadow DOM is no boundary at all. (§9.2) |
| D14 | Nightly compat matrix against real catalog plugins | Trust semver discipline | Catches consequences, not just mistakes. The only mechanism that keeps the compat promise. (§11.5) |

## 19. Open questions

1. **A5 (large result sets)** is the assumption most worth confirming. If reports are typically under
   ~1M rows, the shared-memory Arrow path (§10.4) is over-engineering and could be deferred to
   Phase 3+ — worth roughly two engineer-weeks in Phase 2.
2. **Plugin-authored scheduled jobs.** `trigger` is in the v1 catalog, but a plugin that can schedule
   arbitrary work needs a quota model we haven't designed. Options: cut `trigger` from v1, or limit
   it to host-owned schedules a plugin can only subscribe to. Leaning toward the latter.
3. **Client-surface versioning skew.** A browser holding a report open across a host deploy may have
   a stale plugin bundle. Proposal: version the frame URL (already done) and have the host signal a
   soft reload on skew. Needs a decision before Phase 2.
4. **Native addon policy.** Currently "sign-off required." If a team needs an ODBC driver this gets
   real — per-platform artifacts, and a crash-containment story that only works because of D1.
5. **Per-tenant resource fairness.** §9.1.3 limits are per plugin, not per tenant. One tenant's giant
   query can consume a plugin's whole concurrency budget. Needs a fair-share scheduler in Phase 4 if
   we see it.

## 20. Appendix: glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Extension point** | A named, versioned contract a plugin can implement (`datasource`, `visualization`, …) |
| **Contribution** | A concrete implementation of an extension point by a specific plugin |
| **FQID** | Fully-qualified contribution ID: `<pluginId>/<point>/<localId>` |
| **Capability** | A revocable handle granting a specific external power (HTTP to one host, KV storage) |
| **Capability flag** | A named host feature a plugin can require or feature-detect at handshake |
| **Grant** | An operator's approval of a manifest-declared permission |
| **Trust tier** | `core` / `verified` / `community` — determines isolation and grant policy |
| **Channel** | `canary` / `beta` / `stable` — a promotion track in the catalog |
| **Broker** | Host component that mints and revokes capabilities, and proxies secret use |
| **Reconciler** | Controller loop driving actual plugin state toward desired state |
| **Quarantine** | Terminal-until-operator-action state after repeated crashes |

# Reporting Tool — Plugin Architecture

**Assumptions** (empty working dir, no code to conform to — flagging these since they're load-bearing):

| # | Assumption | What depends on it |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | TypeScript/Node 20+ host | Sandbox mechanics, RPC transport only |
| A2 | Browser rendering surface for reports | Client-surface design |
| A3 | Multi-tenant SaaS + self-hosted SKU | Tenancy model |
| A4 | Plugin authors are internal/partner teams, not the open internet | Trust model |
| A5 | **Result sets can exceed memory** | The data plane. Most worth confirming — if reports are typically <1M rows, that chapter is over-built. |

**Not on Node?** Registry, manifest, lifecycle, versioning, permissions, and governance transfer unchanged. Only the sandbox and transport chapters change — and the conclusion "isolate in a separate OS process" holds on JVM and Python too, for the same reason.

---

## 1. Goals / non-goals

**Goals:** five teams ship independently without cross-coordination · a broken plugin cannot break the host · **unload actually unloads** (this drives the biggest decision in the design) · API breakage is mechanically detectable, not a matter of care · least authority by default · large result sets stream.

**Non-goals, deliberately:** arbitrary marketplace plugins (designed for, not built — needs the WASM tier) · plugins extending the query planner or storage engine · a transitive dependency solver (we are not building npm) · hot-patching in place · direct plugin-to-plugin calls.

---

## 2. Trust model

Tiers are declared in the manifest, **verified by signature**, never self-asserted at runtime.

| Tier | Who | Isolation | Grants |
|---|---|---|---|
| `core` | Platform team, ships in host image | In-process allowed | Implicit |
| `verified` | Your five teams; reviewed, signed | Process isolation | Manifest-declared, operator-approved |
| `community` | Future: external | Process + WASM | Per-grant, egress default-deny |

v1 ships `core` and `verified`.

**In scope:** accidental resource exhaustion, accidental exfiltration, crash/hang including native code, cross-tenant blast radius, supply-chain drift.

**Out of scope, and say this to whoever signs the security review:** a `verified` author who is *deliberately* malicious. The process boundary raises the cost of accidents and casual misbehavior enormously; it is not a hostile-code boundary without WASM. The most common way this design fails in practice is someone reading "sandbox" and assuming a property we didn't build.

---

## 3. Two surfaces, one model

A reporting tool has two execution environments, and pretending otherwise yields two incompatible half-designs.

- **Server surface** — datasource, transform, exporter, destination, trigger. Process isolation.
- **Client surface** — visualization, panel-editor, formatter, theme. Origin isolation.

They share one manifest, one lifecycle state machine, one permission model, one versioning policy, one error taxonomy, one RPC envelope. One package may contribute to both (a Snowflake connector + its connection editor) — that's the common case and must not require two packages.

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ HOST PROCESS (trusted)                                     │
│  planner · tenant auth · secret store · egress proxy       │
│  registry · supervisor · capability broker                 │
└────────┬───────────────────────────────┬───────────────────┘
    IPC ─│─ trust boundary ─│─ postMessage ─ trust boundary
┌────────▼────────────────┐   ┌──────────▼──────────────────┐
│ PLUGIN PROCESS          │   │ PLUGIN IFRAME               │
│ per plugin, untrusted   │   │ null origin, untrusted      │
│ no ambient fs/net       │   │ no network, no cookies      │
└─────────────────────────┘   └─────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## 4. Extension points

`datasource` · `transform` · `exporter` · `destination` · `trigger` (server) — `visualization` · `panel-editor` · `formatter` · `theme` (client).

**Contribution identity:** `<pluginId>/<point>/<localId>`, e.g. `com.acme.snowflake/datasource/snowflake`. Namespacing makes identity collisions structurally impossible, so the registry needs no conflict-resolution policy — only ordering. Saved reports reference the FQID plus the major they were authored against, which is what makes a report portable across installs.

### 4.1 `datasource` — the one with real content

The naive interface is `query(sql) → rows`. That's wrong for reporting, because the planner must know what it can safely push down.

```ts
interface DataSourceCapabilities {
  pushdown: {
    filter: ('eq'|'neq'|'lt'|'lte'|'gt'|'gte'|'in'|'like'|'isNull'|'between')[];
    projection: boolean;
    sort: boolean;
    limit: boolean;
    aggregate: ('count'|'sum'|'avg'|'min'|'max'|'countDistinct'|'percentile')[];
    groupBy: boolean;
    join: 'none' | 'inner' | 'all';
  };
  streaming: boolean;          // false ⇒ host buffers, enforces a lower row cap
  exactRowCount: boolean;
  maxConcurrentQueries: number;
  supportsCancellation: boolean;
  costEstimation: boolean;
  incremental: boolean;        // cursor-based refresh
}
```

Three rules keep this honest:

- **The conformance kit verifies the promise** — it issues each declared pushdown and diffs against host-side reference execution. A plugin claiming `percentile` and computing it wrong fails CI, not production.
- **Under-declaring is always safe** (host falls back to local execution). Over-declaring is a conformance failure.
- `streaming: false` is allowed but capped at `maxBufferedRows` (default 1M), past which the user gets a message naming the plugin.

```jsonc
    "network": { "egress": [
      { "host": "*.snowflakecomputing.com", "ports": [443],
        "reason": "Warehouse query API", "tlsPin": "sha256/…" }
    ]},
    "filesystem": [],                       // empty = none. No implicit temp dir.
    "secrets": [{ "key": "snowflake.credentials", "access": "broker" }],
    "hostApis": ["storage.kv", "telemetry.metrics"]
  },

  "activation": { "events": ["onDataSource:com.acme.snowflake/datasource/snowflake"],
                  "eager": false, "timeoutMs": 10000 },

  "lifecycle": { "concurrentUpgrade": false, "idleTimeoutSec": 900,
                 "drainTimeoutMs": 30000, "isolation": "shared" },

  "resources": { "memoryMb": 512, "cpuMillicores": 1000, "callTimeoutMs": 30000,
                 "maxConcurrency": 8, "egressBytesPerRunMb": 2048,
                 "maxResultRows": 10000000 },

  "configuration": { "$ref": "./schemas/settings.json" },
  "dependencies": { "plugins": [{ "id": "com.acme.oauth-common", "range": "^1.2" }] },
  "integrity": { "signature": "…", "digest": "sha256:…", "sbom": "sbom.spdx.json",
                 "builtBy": "ci://…" }     // populated by the pipeline; author values overwritten
}
```

### Validation rules JSON Schema can't express (second pass)

| Rule | Enforced at | Failure |
|---|---|---|
| `id` within the signing identity's namespace | publish | reject |
| `version` strictly > highest on the channel | publish | reject |
| Client points present iff `runtime.client` present | publish | reject |
| Every egress `reason` ≥ 10 chars | publish | reject — this is a review artifact, not decoration |
| `eager: true` carries an approval token | publish | reject |
| Plugin dep graph acyclic, depth ≤ 2 | install | reject |
| `api.host` satisfiable by this host | install + load | `E_API_INCOMPATIBLE` |
| `resources.memoryMb` ≤ tenant budget | install | reject, naming remaining budget |
| Manifest digest matches signature | install + load | **quarantine** |
| `configuration` is valid 2020-12, no external `$ref` | publish | reject |

Key schema details worth calling out: egress `host` pattern permits exact names or single-level wildcards but **rejects bare `*`**; `access: "plaintext"` on a secret conditionally requires a `signoff` token (JSON Schema `if`/`then`); all package paths are validated against traversal with `^(?!/)(?!.*\.\.)[A-Za-z0-9._/-]+$`.

## 6. Distribution registry (catalog)

**Package format** — gzipped tar, content-addressed: `plugin.json`, `dist/server.js`, `dist/client.js`, `schemas/`, `assets/`, `sbom.spdx.json`.

**Plugins ship bundled. No `node_modules`, no install-time resolution, no postinstall scripts, ever.** Bundling at publish is what makes the artifact reproducible and the SBOM meaningful, and it eliminates "transitive dep changed under us" entirely. Native addons are the one exception: platform sign-off plus per-platform artifacts.

```
GET  /v1/plugins                                list/filter
GET  /v1/plugins/{id}/versions/{v}/manifest     cheap, for resolution
GET  /v1/plugins/{id}/versions/{v}/package      tarball
POST /v1/plugins/{id}/versions                  publish — signed, CI identity only
POST /v1/plugins/{id}/versions/{v}/yank
GET  /v1/index                                  ETag'd, for air-gapped mirroring
```

**Channels:** `canary → beta → stable`. A version is **promoted, not republished** — identical digest across channels, which is what lets you prove the thing you tested is the thing you shipped.

**Yank ≠ delete.** Versions are never deleted. Yanking blocks new installs and alerts on existing ones; it does not auto-uninstall, because silently removing a data source breaks every report using it. `security`-severity yanks can force-quarantine across tenants — audited, two-person approval.

**Air-gapped:** mirror the index + tarballs; signatures verify against a key pinned in the host image, so you don't have to trust the mirror.

## 7. Runtime registry

```ts
interface PluginRecord {
  id: PluginId; version: SemVer; manifest: Manifest;
  source: { channel; digest; installedAt; installedBy };
  state: LifecycleState;
  stateReason?: { code: ErrorCode; message: string; at: Date };
  grants: PermissionGrant[];        // what the operator approved ⊆ what the manifest asked
  instances: InstanceRef[];
  health: { crashes: CrashRecord[]; breaker: BreakerState; lastHealthyAt?: Date };
  contributions: ContributionRecord[];
}
```

**Contribution index:** `Map<ExtensionPointId, ContributionRecord[]>`, sorted. Ordering must be **deterministic across restarts and across cluster nodes** — otherwise two app servers render the same report differently, which is a genuinely miserable bug to chase. Sort key: `(operator order, manifest priority, pluginId, localId)`. The tail is total, so ties never fall through to insertion order.

**Resolution:**
1. Look up FQID → else `E_EXTENSION_NOT_FOUND`, naming the missing plugin (becomes an "install the Snowflake plugin" prompt, not a stack trace).
2. Compare report's authored-against major vs installed: same → proceed; installed newer → proceed + compat annotation; installed older → `E_API_INCOMPATIBLE` naming both versions.
3. Check tenant enablement and grants.

**Plugin deps resolve at install, not load** — walk, check range, reject on cycle or depth > 2. No backtracking, no auto-co-installation. Deliberately 10% of npm's power for 1% of its complexity; for five internal teams that's the right trade.

**Reconciliation.** The registry never mutates plugin processes directly. Desired state in the DB, a controller loop diffs against actual and drives the supervisor. Buys three things: crash recovery is just "reconcile on boot", cluster nodes converge without a coordination protocol, and every transition has one code path to test.

## 8. Lifecycle

```
Discovered ──validate+verify sig──► Resolved ──operator grants──► Installed
                                                                      │ activation event
                                                                      ▼
                                   ┌──────── Activating ◄──backoff─── Crashed
                                   │              │                      ▲
                                   │       activate() ok                 │ crash
                                   ▼              ▼                      │
                              Quarantined ◄──breaker── Active ───────────┘
                              (no restarts)            │  ▲
                                                 drain │  │ reload
                                                       ▼  │
                                                 Deactivating
   Failed = terminal for this version (validation / compat)
```

### Hooks

```ts
interface PluginModule {
  activate(ctx: PluginContext): void | Promise<void>;
  deactivate?(reason: DeactivateReason): void | Promise<void>;   // 'shutdown'|'reload'|'uninstall'
  onConfigChange?(next, prev): void | Promise<void>;             // |'idle'|'quarantine'|'upgrade'
  onUpgrade?(from, to, store: MigrationStore): Promise<void>;
  healthCheck?(): Promise<HealthStatus>;
}
```

Plugins are expected to branch on `DeactivateReason` — flushing a write buffer is right for `shutdown`, pointless for `quarantine`.

**Install/uninstall hooks do not exist, by design.** A plugin that runs code at install time fails in ways operators can't debug, and it's the mechanism behind most real package-manager compromises. Anything you'd want there belongs in `activate` behind a first-run check.

### Load

Lazy by default. Activation events: `onDataSource:<fqid>`, `onExtension:<fqid>`, `onSchedule`, `onStartup` (eager — requires sign-off, counts against a per-tenant budget).

```
1. supervisor.ensureProcess()      spawn if cold
2. handshake                       version + capability negotiation (§11.2)
3. broker.mintCapabilities(grants) handles, not ambient access
4. rpc.call('activate', ctx)       deadline: activation.timeoutMs
5. collect registrations           bound to the plugin's DisposableStore
6. state → Active, index contributions
```

Activation is **idempotent and single-flight** — concurrent runs needing a cold plugin join one promise. Getting this wrong produces double-spawn under load, the classic way plugin systems blow their memory budget during a traffic spike.

### Unload — where most plugin architectures quietly fail

```
1. mark contributions unavailable   → no NEW calls routed
2. drain in-flight                  → min(remaining deadlines, 30s)
3. rpc.call('deactivate', reason)   → 5s
4. broker.revokeAll()               → handles die; in-flight host calls get E_PERMISSION_REVOKED
5. disposables.disposeAll()         → host-side registrations released
6. supervisor.stop()                → SIGTERM, SIGKILL after 5s
```

Steps 4–6 are **the** argument for process isolation. In-process unload cannot be made correct: a plugin that called `setInterval` and lost the handle, opened a socket in a native addon, or captured a module-level reference leaks past any `delete require.cache` you attempt. Step 6 makes unload a guarantee rather than a hope. Anything not backed by `kill(pid)` is best-effort by construction.

Host-side defense for what we *can* control: every registration API returns a `Disposable`; `ctx.subscriptions` auto-disposes; `ctx.signal` (`AbortSignal`) fires at step 3.

### Reload

Deactivate + activate, with two refinements:

- **State handoff.** `deactivate('reload')` may return a JSON blob ≤256 KB, passed to the next `activate` as `ctx.previousState`. For warm caches and pool hints — never correctness-critical state, because reload can fail between halves and the blob is dropped. The conformance kit tests behavior when it's absent.
- **Drain-before-swap upgrades.** New process activates → registry atomically swaps routing → old drains and exits. In-flight runs finish on the old version. Opt-in via `lifecycle.concurrentUpgrade` (default false) since a plugin holding an exclusive external lock can't tolerate two instances.

**Dev hot reload** (file watch, 200–400ms) is the highest-leverage DX feature in the system, and it falls out for free because unload actually works.

### Crash supervision

Breaker trips at 5 crashes / 10 min, **or 3 consecutive crashes within 30s of activation**. The second condition matters — a plugin dying immediately on activation would otherwise burn the full backoff schedule before tripping. Backoff `min(1s·2ⁿ, 60s)` ±20% jitter.

Retry policy: `query`/`describe`/`plan`/`testConnection` are idempotent, retried once. `transform.apply` only if `pure: true`. **`destination.deliver` is never auto-retried without an `idempotencyKey`** — double-emailing a board report is worse than failing.

**Quarantine:** contributions hidden, no restarts, dependent reports fail with a message naming the plugin, operator alert. Exit requires explicit action or a version upgrade. Recorded centrally, so a plugin crash-looping on one node doesn't silently keep serving from another.

## 9. The sandbox

### 9.1 Decision: separate OS process. Not `vm`, not `vm2`, not worker threads.

This is the load-bearing decision, so — the full reasoning:

- **Node's `vm` is explicitly not a security boundary.** Node's own docs say so. Constructor-chain escapes (`this.constructor.constructor('return process')()`) have been rediscovered continuously for a decade.
- **`vm2` is dead** — discontinued in 2023 after a series of escape CVEs its author judged unfixable in the design. Anything built on it today is built on a known-broken foundation.
- **Worker threads share the process.** You get `resourceLimits` for heap, but a worker can still call `process.exit()`, and a native addon segfault takes the host with it. Disqualifying for requirement #2.
- **A separate process** gives OS-enforced memory limits, real CPU accounting, kill-means-kill unload, crash containment including native code, and a natural place to drop privileges.

The cost is IPC serialization on the hot path — which is exactly why §10.4 exists.

**What a plugin process gets** (one per plugin per node):

- **Clean env** — allowlist only (`NODE_ENV`, `TZ`, `LANG`, channel FD). No inherited secrets, no `AWS_*`, no proxy vars.
- **Linux:** dedicated uid, `no_new_privs`, seccomp blocking `socket(2)`/`connect(2)` outright (all network goes through the broker), cgroup v2 memory + CPU, read-only rootfs, per-plugin tmpfs.
- **Windows:** Job Object with `ProcessMemoryLimit`, `KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE`, `ActiveProcessLimit = 1`, restricted token, per-plugin temp dir.
- **Node flags:** `--max-old-space-size` matched to the manifest, `--disallow-code-generation-from-strings`, `--frozen-intrinsics`, `--experimental-permission` denying fs/net/child_process as defense in depth.
- **No console stdio** — captured, line-bounded, rate-limited, forwarded as structured records tagged with the plugin ID. A plugin logging 100 MB/s gets throttled and flagged, not allowed to fill the node's disk.

**The plugin process enforces nothing.** It is untrusted. Every limit above is imposed from outside by the OS or the host. That's the property that makes the boundary real.

**Resource governance:**

| Limit | Mechanism | On breach |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | cgroup / Job Object + heap flag | OOM-kill → crash path |
| CPU | cgroup `cpu.max` / JO rate | Throttle; sustained → `E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` |
| Wall clock/call | Host-side deadline | Cancel, `E_TIMEOUT`, strike |
| Concurrency | Host-side semaphore | Queue, then exhausted |
| Egress bytes | Broker accounting | Hard stop mid-stream |
| Result rows | Data plane counter | `E_RESULT_TOO_LARGE` |
| Log volume | Token bucket | Drop + flag |
| Process count | `ActiveProcessLimit` / pids cgroup | `fork` fails inside plugin |

**Three timeout strikes in 5 min recycles the process** — repeated timeouts usually mean a leak or deadlock, and recycling is cheaper than diagnosing it live.

**WASM tier (designed, Phase 4).** For a future `community` tier: WASM components under WASI Preview 2 — capability-based by construction, deterministic, memory-safe, ms cold start. Not v1 because the "TypeScript → WASM component" toolchain is workable but the story for a connector wanting a mature DB driver is not. **The API contract in §11 is deliberately WASM-shaped** — no shared mutable state, everything through explicit capability handles, all data as serializable buffers — so this is additive, not a rewrite. *Do not add a host API taking a callback with shared state; it closes this door.*

### 9.2 Client surface

Different threat model: not resource exhaustion but access to the host page — session cookies, other tenants' rendered data, surrounding DOM.

```html
<iframe
  sandbox="allow-scripts"        <!-- NOT allow-same-origin -->
  csp="default-src 'none'; script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval';
       style-src 'unsafe-inline'; img-src data: blob:"
  referrerpolicy="no-referrer" allow=""
  src="https://plugin-cdn.example/com.acme.snowflake/2.3.1/frame.html">
```

`allow-scripts` **without** `allow-same-origin` is the critical detail — together they let the frame reach into the parent and strip its own sandbox attribute. Null origin means no cookies, no shared storage, no cross-boundary DOM.

Plus: separate CDN origin per plugin · `postMessage` only, origin-checked both ends with a per-frame handshake nonce · data arrives as **transferred** (zero-copy) Arrow `ArrayBuffer`s · a frame exceeding `frameBudgetMs` for N consecutive frames is suspended with a visible "this visualization is slow" state rather than freezing the report · **no network from the client surface, ever** — CSP `default-src 'none'`, no `connect-src`. A chart that can make arbitrary requests carrying the user's session is an exfiltration primitive.

Interactions (tooltip, brush, drilldown) go host-ward over the same channel, so the host controls what a click can trigger.

### 9.3 Capability broker

No ambient authority. Every external interaction is a handle minted at activation, scoped to approved grants, revoked at deactivation.

```ts
interface HttpCapability { fetch(req): Promise<PluginResponse>; }      // allowlisted + accounted
interface StorageCapability {                                          // (plugin, tenant)-namespaced
  get(key): Promise<Uint8Array | undefined>;
  set(key, value, opts?: { ttlSec?: number }): Promise<void>;
  list(prefix): AsyncIterable<string>;
}
```

Handles are revocable by construction: the host holds the implementation, the plugin holds a proxy ID. Revocation flips a bit host-side — a plugin that stashed a handle in a closure gains nothing, and revocation works even against a process ignoring its `AbortSignal`.

### 9.4 Secrets

| Mode | Plugin gets | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| **`broker`** (default) | Nothing — it says "sign this with `snowflake.credentials`"; the host injects at the egress proxy | Almost always |
| `token` | Short-lived (≤15 min), narrowly scoped | An SDK demands a credential object |
| `plaintext` | The value | Last resort; sign-off recorded in the manifest |

Under `broker`, a fully compromised plugin still cannot exfiltrate the credential — it can only cause requests to an allowlisted host, a dramatically smaller problem. Secrets never appear in env vars, the manifest, or plugin stdio, and a host-side scrubber keyed on actual values redacts them from logs and errors as a backstop.

### 9.5 Egress proxy

All plugin traffic routes through it — and since the process can't call `connect(2)` at all, that's OS-enforced, not cooperative. The proxy: matches the allowlist · **blocks private/link-local ranges after DNS resolution** (stops SSRF via DNS rebinding) · pins TLS where declared · injects brokered credentials · counts bytes against the run cap · rate-limits · writes an audit record per request.

## 10. Wire protocol

**Transport:** Unix socket (Linux/macOS) · named pipe (Windows) · `postMessage` with Transferables (client). 4-byte BE length prefix, max 8 MB control frame.

**Control plane:** JSON-RPC 2.0 shape, **MessagePack** encoding (~2–4× faster/smaller than JSON, and it has a real binary type, which matters when payloads carry Arrow buffers).

```jsonc
{ "id": 42, "method": "datasource.query",
  "params": { "connectionRef": "cap:conn:7f3a", "query": {…} },
  "meta": { "traceId": "…", "tenantId": "t_123",
            "deadlineUnixMs": 1737000030000, "apiVersion": "1.4" } }

{ "id": 42, "error": { "code": "E_UPSTREAM", "retryable": true, "retryAfterMs": 5000,
    "message": "Snowflake: warehouse suspended",
    "userMessage": "The warehouse is paused. Ask your admin to resume it." } }
```

Bidirectional on one channel, independent ID spaces per direction. **Deadlines are absolute timestamps, not durations** — a queued call doesn't get a fresh budget. Subtle, but it's what prevents deadline amplification in chained calls.

**Cancellation:** `$cancel` notification; the host doesn't wait forever for the courtesy — deadline + 2s grace, then abandon; three abandonments recycles the process. Cancellation propagates transitively by `traceId`.

### 10.4 Data plane — makes or breaks a reporting tool's plugin system

- **Apache Arrow IPC.** Columnar, zero-copy readable, language-agnostic, real type system including decimals and timestamp-with-tz. A reporting plugin boundary moves tabular data; JSON costs roughly an order of magnitude in both CPU and bytes.
- **Batched** — 64K rows or 16 MB, whichever first. Schema sent once at stream open.
- **Credit-based backpressure.** Consumer grants credits; producer may not exceed them. Without this, a fast source into a slow transform buffers unboundedly in the host and you learn about it via an OOM at 2 a.m.
- **Shared memory for big payloads** (`memfd` / named shared memory), control frame carries only a handle — a 16 MB batch crosses as a pointer, not a copy. This claws back most of the cost of process isolation.

```
host ── query(req) ──────────────────► plugin
     ◄─ $stream.open {streamId, schema}
     ── $stream.credit {n: 4} ───────►
     ◄─ $stream.batch {shm: …} ×4
     ── $stream.credit {n: 4} ───────►
     ◄─ $stream.end {rows, stats}
```

## 11. Versioned API contract

**One semver number** covers the `PluginContext` surface, every extension point interface, the wire protocol, and the error taxonomy. Not per-point versioning — five teams should reason about one compatibility question, not nine.

| Change | Bump |
|---|---|
| New extension point / optional method / optional field / error code | **minor** |
| Remove, rename, retype, tighten validation, change semantics | **major** |
| Docs, perf, contract-preserving fix | patch |

**Support window: major N and N−1, minimum two quarters after N ships.** That's the promise to the five teams: at least six months to migrate, never a forced same-sprint upgrade.

### Handshake — the only place negotiation happens

```
host   → { hostApiVersions: ["1.4","2.1"], capabilities: [...], hostVersion: "2026.9.1" }
plugin → { selected: "1.4", requires: [...], provides: ["datasource","panel-editor"] }
host   → verify selected ∈ offered ∧ manifest.api.host satisfies it ∧ requires ⊆ capabilities
         else E_API_INCOMPATIBLE → Failed, message naming both versions
```

No per-call version fields, no runtime sniffing of host internals. A plugin that can't get what it needs fails loudly at activation, not subtly at render time.

### Capability flags — how additive change actually works

New functionality within a major arrives as a capability flag, never a silent behavior change:

```ts
if (ctx.hasCapability('datasource.costEstimate')) {
  registry.registerDataSource({ ...spec, estimateCost });
}
```

One build runs against host 1.4 and 1.9 with no version-string conditionals — which are always wrong eventually, because the thing you care about is the feature, not the number.

### Deprecation

Minor N: `@deprecated` in the `.d.ts` with replacement + removal version; one-time structured runtime warning, never a throw. Minor N+1: also surfaces in the admin UI and health status. Major N+1: removed. **Migration guide and codemod publish at deprecation time, not at removal.** Minimum two minors and one full quarter. No exceptions without an RFC and direct notice to every affected owner — the catalog knows who they are, so "we didn't know who was using it" is never acceptable.

### Mechanical enforcement (care doesn't scale to five teams)

1. API extractor rolls the public surface into a committed `.api.md`.
2. A PR changing that file **fails** without a matching version bump and an `api-change:minor|major` label (major requires an RFC link).
3. Semver linting classifies the diff and cross-checks the declared bump. Removed method on a minor = hard failure.
4. **Nightly compatibility matrix:** every `stable`-channel plugin runs against host `main`. Breaking the five teams shows up as a red build on *our* repo, not as their incident.
5. Protocol golden files replay recorded wire traces to catch serialization breakage types can't see.

Item 4 is the one that actually keeps the promise. The rest catch mistakes; that catches consequences.

## 12. Errors and observability

| Code | Retryable | Fault | Surfaced as |
|---|---|---|---|
| `E_MANIFEST_INVALID` | no | author | publish/install failure |
| `E_API_INCOMPATIBLE` | no | author/operator | both versions named |
| `E_PERMISSION_DENIED` | no | operator | admin grant prompt |
| `E_USER_CONFIG` | no | end user | inline field error |
| `E_UPSTREAM` | usually | external | "Snowflake unavailable" + retry-after |
| `E_TIMEOUT` | yes | plugin/upstream | names the plugin |
| `E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` | maybe | plugin/query | "add a filter" |
| `E_RESULT_TOO_LARGE` | no | end user | cap + current count |
| `E_PLUGIN_CRASHED` | if idempotent | author | generic message + operator alert |
| `E_INTERNAL` | no | platform | generic + our alert |

**Two messages per error, always.** `userMessage` is end-user-safe and actionable; `message` + `details` go to operators. A plugin putting a connection string in `userMessage` fails conformance; host-side redaction is the backstop for paths conformance can't reach.

**Telemetry**, all tagged `(pluginId, version, point, tenantId, traceId)`: `plugin_call_duration_ms`, `plugin_call_errors_total`, `plugin_activation_duration_ms`, `plugin_memory_rss_bytes`, `plugin_cpu_seconds_total`, `plugin_crashes_total`, `plugin_egress_bytes_total`, `plugin_rows_emitted_total`, **`plugin_stream_credit_wait_ms`** (backpressure visibility — the early warning for a slow plugin), `plugin_state`.

Host span context propagates into the plugin, so one trace shows planning → plugin query → upstream → transform. That's the difference between "the report is slow" and "the Snowflake plugin spends 8 seconds in DNS." **Per-plugin dashboards are generated from a template at install** — five teams, five identical debugging experiences.
